story.headline: A far stronger US jobs report than expected gave the dollar its biggest daily gain in nearly five months and made a December Fed rate hike likely again. Gold, the Aussie and the kiwi fell.

reads.policy: The strong US jobs report made a December Federal Reserve hike the market's main expectation again, which firms up the dollar's rate support. Most other big central banks still lean toward hiking, but Canada's job losses and weak European spending give their banks reasons to go slower. For now the rate story tilts toward the dollar.
reads.growth: The US job market is much firmer than it looked, while Canada lost jobs for a second month and euro-area shoppers cut back. That split favours the dollar over the loonie and the euro. A long stock slump could still weigh on spending if it lasts.
reads.inflation: Faster US pay growth adds to inflation worries, though households expect prices to rise a little less than before. Oil slipped back below $100, so the energy push has eased this week. Next Tuesday's US inflation figures are the next big check.
reads.risk: The AI and chip-stock selloff hit Asia hard, then US chip stocks bounced, so the panic eased without reversing. The Aussie and the kiwi still fell hardest, while the yen and the franc held up against them. Fear and higher US yields together left the dollar the day's clear winner.
reads.tot: Oil briefly topped $100 on new tanker attacks, then slipped back as hopes of more Middle East supply held. Cheaper oil this week eases the bill for importers like Japan and the euro area. It also takes away some support from the Canadian dollar.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the Canadian dollar, so Friday's slide in the loonie went their way. They still lean toward the Aussie while real-money investors bet heavily against it, and the Aussie's fall this week hurts the funds' side. Fresh figures came out this afternoon and will show here once processed.
reads.fiscal: No new budget news moved currencies on Friday. A Democratic Congress makes President Trump's spending plans harder to pass, a mild drag on the dollar that the jobs report overshadowed. France's debt worries still weigh on the euro.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike. A far stronger October jobs report has made a December hike the market's main expectation again.
fed.why: US inflation is running well above the Fed's 2% goal, and October brought strong hiring and faster pay growth. That tells the Fed the economy can handle another hike.
fed.watch: US inflation figures for October on Tuesday at 7:30 AM CT: hot prices would make a December hike close to certain, while a soft reading would revive doubts. The decision is December 9.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October and has said more hikes may be needed. Canada's second straight month of job losses makes a December hike less certain.
boc.priced: December: further hike about even odds before Friday's weak jobs figures.
boc.why: Dearer energy is lifting Canadian inflation, but the job market keeps weakening and pay growth is cooling. That gives the bank reasons to move slowly.
boc.watch: Canada's October inflation figures later this month and oil prices, before the December 9 decision.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a 4–3 vote, though members agreed more tightening is likely. Rising unemployment has cut bets on a December hike to below even.
rbnz.priced: December: hike less likely than not.
rbnz.why: Price pressures argue for a hike, but unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for patience.
rbnz.watch: Saturday's general election and whether the new government changes the budget outlook, before the December 9 decision.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held its deposit rate at 2.50% in October, and markets expect a hike in December. Its leaders stress that energy is the main cause of high inflation and that the data will decide.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the goal, mostly because of energy, but shoppers are cutting back and borrowing costs have already risen. That makes the bank wary of doing too much.
ecb.watch: Euro-area data between now and the December 17 decision, when new staff forecasts arrive.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan held at 1.25% in October, and markets expect a hike in December. Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Friday that real interest rates have not risen much, leaving room to act.
boj.why: The bank judges underlying inflation close to its 2% goal, and a weak yen keeps import prices high.
boj.watch: Wage and price figures and any comments from Ueda before the December 18 decision.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest since 2008, but three members wanted to wait. Governor Michele Bullock hinted at a pause to take stock.
rba.priced: December: no firm pricing yet; the bank itself hinted at a pause.
rba.why: Inflation is too high on every measure, but the economy is slowing and unemployment is at a five-year high.
rba.watch: Australian jobs and spending figures, and the global stock mood, before the December 8 decision.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5, its first hike since 2023, in an 8–1 vote where the dissenter wanted a bigger move. Governor Andrew Bailey said it is unlikely to be the last unless the Middle East conflict ends.
boe.priced: December: a second hike possible; no firm pricing yet.
boe.why: UK inflation is at its highest in about a year on energy and fuel costs, and the bank expects it to climb further.
boe.watch: UK monthly growth figures next week and October inflation figures later this month, before the December 17 decision.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and says it can still sell francs if needed. Swiss inflation rose to 1.5% in October, which makes another cut less likely.
snb.priced: December: hold expected, though pricing is mixed.
snb.why: Inflation is inside the bank's 0–2% range but rising on fuel, while a strong franc keeps import prices down.
snb.watch: The franc's strength against the euro and any intervention signals before the December 10 decision.

USD.summary: The dollar sits in the middle of the board: rate and inflation support are partly offset by a Democratic Congress. A strong October jobs report revived bets that the Federal Reserve hikes in December.

notes.policy: A December Fed hike is again the market's main expectation after hiring beat forecasts by a wide margin.
notes.inflation: US inflation is well above the Fed's goal, and faster pay growth keeps the pressure on.
notes.fiscal: With Democrats controlling Congress, President Trump's spending plans look harder to pass, which trims some support for the dollar.

EUR.summary: The euro sits near the bottom of the board: dear energy hurts Europe's economy, growth is uneven and France's debt worries linger. Its main cushion is that speculators already bet heavily against it.

notes.policy: The European Central Bank is expected to hike in December, but its leaders sound in no hurry, so its rate support is softer than elsewhere.
notes.growth: Euro-area growth is uneven, and shoppers cut spending sharply in September.
notes.inflation: Inflation is about double the bank's goal, which keeps a December hike in view.
notes.tot: Europe imports most of its energy, so high oil prices drain money out of the region.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold one of their biggest bets against the euro in years, so good news could set off a quick unwind.
notes.fiscal: France's debt and budget troubles weigh on confidence in the euro.

GBP.summary: The pound sits at the top of the board: the Bank of England has just started hiking, UK inflation is high and business surveys have held up. Speculators still bet heavily against it, which leaves room for a quick unwind.

notes.policy: The Bank of England raised rates on November 5 and signalled more may follow.
notes.growth: UK business surveys have been firm, even though shoppers are cautious.
notes.inflation: UK inflation is at its highest in about a year, keeping pressure on the bank.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold one of their biggest bets against the pound in 20 years, so good news can force a quick unwind.

JPY.summary: The yen sits near the bottom of the board because Japanese rates are far below others and Japan pays more for imported energy. Fear in stock markets is its main support.

notes.policy: Japanese rates remain far below other countries' even with a December hike likely, which keeps money flowing out of the yen.
notes.risk: The yen draws money when markets get scared, as they did this week when chip stocks slumped.
notes.tot: Japan imports almost all its energy, so dear oil weighs on the yen.
notes.positioning: Speculators already hold one of their biggest bets on the yen in 20 years, which leaves room for a sharp unwind if fear fades.

CHF.summary: The franc sits mid-board: it draws money when markets are nervous, but Swiss inflation is low and the central bank holds rates at zero.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is low and inside the central bank's range, which keeps rates at zero and the franc's rate support thin.
notes.risk: The franc gains when investors look for safety, as they did during this week's stock slump.

AUD.summary: The Aussie scores well on the board thanks to Australia's high interest rates, hot inflation and commodity exports. But it trades on the global mood and has fallen hard as stocks slumped.

notes.policy: The Reserve Bank of Australia has the highest rate among the major central banks after its November hike.
notes.growth: Australia's economy is slowing, with unemployment at a five-year high.
notes.inflation: Australian inflation is running hotter than the central bank expected.
notes.tot: Australia exports energy and metals, so firm commodity prices bring money in.
notes.positioning: Big investors overall hold one of their largest bets against the Aussie in 20 years, which can unwind quickly on good news.

CAD.summary: The loonie scores well on the board on the Bank of Canada's hikes, firm price pressures and oil exports. A weakening job market is its soft spot, and it showed on Friday.

notes.policy: The Bank of Canada raised rates in October and has said more may be needed.
notes.growth: Canada lost jobs for a second straight month in October, and unemployment rose.
notes.inflation: Price pressures in the pipeline remain strong, keeping the central bank alert.
notes.tot: Canada exports oil, so higher crude prices bring money into the loonie.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits mid-board: export prices help and speculators already bet heavily against it, but a weak job market has cut bets on a December hike.

notes.growth: New Zealand's job market is weakening, with unemployment at its highest since 2015.
notes.tot: Firm dairy prices support New Zealand's export earnings.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold one of their biggest bets against the kiwi in 20 years, so good news could trigger a quick unwind.
